title: The Chunking Fallacy: Why Native Long-Context Windows Surpass RAG in Scientific Document Synthesis
abstract: Common wisdom assumes that retrieval modules provide clean evidence subsets for LLMs. In this empirical critique, we prove that text chunking irreversibly destroys cross-section discourse structure and inter-paragraph co-reference in scientific literature. On complex academic synthesis queries, full-context attention without retrieval preserves holistic argumentation, yielding higher factual coherence and avoiding retrieval omission errors.

sections.Abstract: Common wisdom assumes that retrieval modules provide clean evidence subsets for LLMs. In this empirical critique, we prove that text chunking irreversibly destroys cross-section discourse structure and inter-paragraph co-reference in scientific literature. On complex academic synthesis queries, full-context attention without retrieval preserves holistic argumentation, yielding higher factual coherence and avoiding retrieval omission errors.
sections.Introduction: Retrieval-augmented architectures enforce an artificial discretization of scientific texts into arbitrary chunks (typically 200-500 words). When evidence requires synthesizing hypotheses from the Introduction with empirical exceptions in the Discussion, top-k retrievers frequently drop the contradictory nuance.
sections.Methodology: We evaluate Claude-3 and LLaMA-3 with 200k native context against state-of-the-art hybrid RAG pipelines on full-length biomedical and NLP manuscripts from SQuAD and MultiHop benchmarks.
sections.Experiments: We measure answer completeness and cross-document reasoning accuracy under varying document lengths (10k to 100k tokens).
sections.Results: Full-context models without retrieval outperform RAG by 4.8% in comprehensive multi-paragraph synthesis, achieving 79.0% F1 compared to 74.2% for chunk-based RAG. When claims rely on subtle caveats buried in appendices, retrieval pipelines fail to recall the qualifying chunk 34% of the time, causing unjustified confidence in partial evidence.
sections.Conclusion: For complex scientific literature, native long-context attention outperforms chunk-based RAG by preserving holistic context and eliminating retriever omission failures.
